content.title: General Comment to the Reviewers
content.comment: We thank the reviewers for their time and thoughtful feedback. We appreciate their assessment of our proposed setting as novel and their suggestions to strengthen the empirical results. We also thank Reviewer uDFQ for taking the time to include extra suggestions beyond the main review. Due to the time expense of running AutoAttack evaluations, we plan to take them and other suggestions into consideration in an updated version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores a new problem, i.e., the generalizability of adversarial robustness under distribution shifts. Specifically, this paper provides the empirical analysis of training robust models on multiple domains and evaluates their accuracy and robustness on unseen domains. The main observations are both empirical and certifiable robustness generalize to unseen domains, and the generalizability does not correlate well with the input visual similarity between the source and target domains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This work explores a new setting, the generalizability of adversarial robustness under distribution shifts.
2. This work provides the empirical analysis of training robust models and evaluating on the unseen domains to check both empirical and certifiable robustness. The empirical analysis provides interesting observations.

Weaknesses:
1. It is unclear why robustness is excepted to be generalizable to the unseen domains if the robustness has the same definition as the traditional one (i.e., robust against the adversarial attack). From another pespective, the example of the environment having the distribution shift can also be viewed as a kind of adversarial example (which are sometimes considered to be the robustness against OOD samples). Could the authors provide the significance and practicability of considering such generalizability? 
2. The explored new setting may need a more rigorous definition and a clear comparison with other problem settings, although the current writing has described it. Following the previous issue, it could be better to present its unique points that are different from distributional adversarial robustness and robustness to OOD samples. This may help to clarify its significance better.
3. It is not very clear what is the major significance of the second main observation, "the level of generalizability does not correlate well with input visual similarity," since it seems to be common sense that visual similarity does not indicate the close correlation in adversarial settings.
4. Some related theoretical analyses may enhance the generalizability and scalability of the current observations.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: most presentation of this work is well and clear. However, in either the empirical or certifiable robustness section, the observations seem to be not very organized. It may be better to remark on or summarize those general phenomena in a specific part of each section.

Quality: this paper present an understanding and exploration work on the generalizability of adversarial robustness in an unseen domain. However, this paper has limited technical contribution. 

Novelty: in my opinion, the empirical exploration of the new setting is novel, considering the existence of literature.

Reproducibility: it seems this paper didn't provide source code or completed experimental information. It is encouraged to provide more details about the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper provides the empirical analysis of a new problem, i.e., the generalizability of adversarial robustness under distribution shift. Currently, my major concern is the significance and practicability of considering such generalizability. It would be better if the authors could provide more discussion on it.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper investigates how well adversarial robustness (both empirical and certified) generalized to unseen domains of the standard domain generalization benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written and covers (as far as I am aware) the relevant standard benchmarks. It does not introduce a new method, which in my opinion benefits it by focussing in detail on investigating the question at hand and providing the reader with a good baseline reference.

I'm not an expert in domain generalization, but from discussions with a colleague, the regarded benchmark and experimental methodology are fine. The investiagtion of adversarial robustness generalization in this field seems to be novel, but I might be missing relevant literature knowledge.

Especially for a paper that is about evaluating adversarial robustness, the current empirical robustness evaluation is too weak, and I do not recommend accepting the paper as long as this issue is not resolved (using at least with AutoAttack [0]). Using one of the available stronger defenses (e.g. TRADES [1] as main empirical defense) would also be important in my opinion. The other one of the issues listed below I would consider minor.

The evaluations of certified robustness look fine (though details on the interpretation of Randomized Smoothing should be adjusted).

Detailed issues:

1. The evaluation of empirial adversarial robustness is not sufficient. It is stated in 4.1 that each model is trained and evaluated with 20 steps of PGD, which is not sufficient for evaluation (see e.g. [0]). Currently, it is standard to at least evaluate with AutoAttack [0], and either add attacks adapted to the specific situation or discuss why no strong adaptive attacks are expected to be constructible.

2. Related to the previous point, the robust accuracies in Figure 1 seem to be unexpectedly high for several instances. ϵ = 0.125 is very high for $l_\infty$ robustness, and some models that are undefended or were trained with much smaller (<=50%) ϵ showing nontrivial robust accuracy looks unrealistic to me. I am not familiar with other adversarial robustness numbers on those datasets, but for the commonly evaluated ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, robust accuracies can only be achieved for radii that are ~8 resp. ~3 times smaller [2].

3. Instead of adversarial training, it would also make sense to use better defenses which have been known for years. TRADES is shown with very few results in the appendix. I see no reason why the main results wouldn't use it.

4. The used datasets should be cited, e.g. [3] for OfficeHome etc., instead of only mentioning the DomainBed benchmark.

5. In 5.1, the discussion of Randomized Smoothing should include the important aspect that the guarantees are of a certain probabilistic nature.

6. Discussing different threat model norms for empirical and certified robustness is not ideal. The discussions in 4.2 only reference $l_\infty$ (right?), but including the finding from the appendix A.2 would be helpful. The qualitative observations are the same, correct? 

7. Whether clean domain generalization accuracy can in general be expected to be benefitting from adversarial training on the source domains does not become clear. The contributions seem contradictory here, once saying that in contrast to transfer learning they it doesn't, and then saying that for the medical application, it does. Due to the statistically speaking small number of tasks, the finding appears to be inconclusive either way. If I am correct here, I think both should not be emphasized as a finding in the contributions.

Suggestions and questions:

- In 3 -- Domain Generalization Setup:
  - It would be helpful to discuss whether or not is is assumed that $P^{(n)}(y|x) = P^{(k)}(y|x)$ for all $n,k$ (with support at $x$), i.e. "Is the shift assumed to be covariate?".
  - Is information to which source domain a training input belongs generally available? (like used in [4])
  - For Eq. (1), in many cases, one is interested in the accuracy on the target domain instead of the cross-entropy to the ground truth. (This would formally be represented by the 0-1-loss, but simpler notations are possible.) Is the choice of seeking minimal cross-entropy deliberate? If so, I think it should be discussed. Usually, the same is done w.r.t. the validation data, by choosing the most accurate model.
  - Empirical risk minimization as described here currently seems to be the most sensible method for domain generalization, as established by [5]; is that a fair assessment? I think it should be discussed in how far that justifies that adversarial robustifications of other methods are not considered.

- I think the central finding that "both empirical and certified robustness generalize to unseen domains" should be included in the contribution list.

- For the related task of distribution shift / corruption robustness, in Appendix F Robustness across distribution shifts of [2] is measured, with similar outcomes. I think a short discussion on this related result would be helpful.

- There might also be some interesting parallels with the generalizability of adversarial empirical [6] and certified [7] robustness of out-of-distribution detection to unseen domains.

- Including a short description of the DomainBed benchmark would be helpful.

- Why is the rest of WILDS not used? (I'm not sure which datasets of the current WILDS are relevant for domain generalization)

- The reason for the different/separate treatments of WILDS CAMELYON17 and the DomainBed tasks does not become clear to me. Is it mostly only about it being a real-world application?

- Showing the clean and (if possible) empirical robust accuracies of the certified models (i.e. the smoothed functions) could be insightful.

[0] Croce and Hein, ICML 2020: "Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks"

[1] Zhang et al., ICML 2019: "Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness and accuracy."

[2] Croce et al., NeurIPS 2021: "RobustBench: a standardized adversarial robustness benchmark"

[3] Venkateswara et al., CVPR 2017: "Deep hashing network for unsupervised domain adaptation."

[4] Zhang et al, ICML 2022: "Correct-N-Contrast: A Contrastive Approach for Improving Robustness to Spurious Correlations"

[5] Gulrajani et al., ICML 2021: "In Search of Lost Domain Generalization"

[6] Hein et al, CVPR 2019: "Why ReLU networks yield high-confidence predictions far away from the training data and how to mitigate the problem"

[7] Bitterwolf et al., NeurIPS 2020: "Certifiably Adversarially Robust Detection of Out-of-Distribution Data"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and quality of the writing and presentation are good.

The quality of the evaluations has an important issue, as detailed above.

While I'm not working in the field of domain generalization, the consideration of adversarial robustness generalization in this field appears to be novel to me.

Investigating the relationship between visual similarity and robustness generalizability seems to be a (but the only) novel methodological contribution.

Not code is provided as far as I am aware. The general experimental methods are described in enough detail to reproduce them, however it is always important to have access to the specific evaluated models in order to compare and explain potential differences of reproduced results with the described ones.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors study whether adversarial robustness generalizes across domains.  They conduct experiments with adversarial training and randomized smoothing defenses and demonstrate that across various datasets for the domain generalization task, being robust on the source also implies robustness on the target domain.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- interesting line of research
- in depth experiments
- writing is clear

Weaknesses:
- the authors show a lot of experimental results, but there isn't much analysis of why we observe this generalization.  My guess is that adversarial training causes the model to learn to be invariant to noise which leads to this trend.  For randomized smoothing techniques this robustness may be the result of the data augmentation used during training.  I would be interested in seeing some experiments with standard training + gaussian noise augmentation and see if the model generalizes to unseen domains with gaussian noise.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation is clear and the experiments are very in depth.  Novelty in technique is somewhat limited since the authors use existing methods and existing datasets, but I think the empirical results are interesting and significant since to the best of my knowledge this is the first work investigating the impact of adversarial robustness on domain generalization.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this is an interesting paper with good scope in experiments, but I think that there is a lack of analysis of why the authors observe certain results.  I am happy to raise my score if the authors address this point more.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how adversarial robust models generalizes to different domains (without fintuning). They first examine the accuracy of the adversarial robust model in the source and target domain. They found the accuracies in these two domains are correlated (without any statistic tests). Next, they look at the certified robustness of the model and found that the certified robustness also transfers. Finally, they applied their findings on one dataset (WILDS CAMELYON17).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The authors tries to bring many evidence to systematically support their claim.

Weaknesses:
- Lack of statistic tests for many conclusions. Hard to know if their conclusion generalizes or is it by chance.
- Many conclusions seems a bit shallow and many meaningful research questions are "left as a future direction".
  - for example, they pointed out higher robustness in the source domain corresponds to higher robustness in the target domain, this is quite trivial as prior work already showed that clean accuracy transfers this way. This would not brought any useful insights without additional analysis. 
- The real world application on medical images seems a bit cherry picked. Why only the CAMELYON17 (the WILDS have many datasets)? why only compare with CORAL (there are many other algorithms for distributional generalization tasks)? How is the robust radius (epsilon = 8/255) chosen (there should be no validation data as they don't even have data for fintuning)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation is clear.

There are no code provided, I cannot say for certain of the reproducibility.

There is a marginal novelty as this is the first time I see comparison between robustness on source and target domain.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper is heading towards a right direction. However, many findings are too shallow and would not be interesting enough. I encourage the author to dig deeper into their findings and study what are the root causes of their observations. Another suggestion is to look into some of the future research questions mentioned in their paper is a good direction too.

content.title: Generalizability of Adversarial Robustness Under Distribution Shifts
content.abstract: Recent progress in empirical and certified robustness promises to deliver reliable and deployable Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Despite that success, most existing evaluations of DNN robustness have been done on images sampled from the same distribution that the model was trained on. Yet, in the real world, DNNs may be deployed in dynamic environments that exhibit significant distribution shifts. In this work, we take a first step towards thoroughly investigating the interplay between empirical and certified adversarial robustness on one hand and domain generalization on another. To do so, we train robust models on multiple domains and evaluate their accuracy and robustness on an unseen domain. We observe that: (1) both empirical and certified robustness generalize to unseen domains, and (2) the level of generalizability does not correlate well with input visual similarity, measured by the FID between source and target domains. We also extend our study to cover a real-world medical application, in which adversarial augmentation enhances both the robustness and generalization accuracy in unseen domains.
